html:
A flood made on purpose in June 1938, when Chinese Nationalist troops broke the dykes of the Yellow River at Huayuankou in Henan to slow the advance of the Japanese army. It killed hundreds of thousands of Chinese civilians.

It was early in the war with Japan. Japanese forces had taken Kaifeng and were moving on Zhengzhou, a key rail junction, on the way to Wuhan. Chiang Kai-shek's government chose to use the river as a weapon. The water poured southeast across the plains of Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu into the Huai River.

The flood did delay the Japanese for some months, but Wuhan still fell that autumn. The cost was immense: estimates of the dead run from about 400,000 to 900,000, and millions lost their homes. The flooded land produced little for years, which fed the Henan famine of 1942. The government at first blamed Japanese bombing. The river was only turned back to its old bed in 1947, with American aid. Like the flood of 1887, it shows how much of north China depends on the river's dykes.
sum: A flood made on purpose in June 1938, when Chinese Nationalist troops broke the dykes of the Yellow River at Huayuankou in Henan to slow the advance of the Japanese army. It killed hundreds of thousands of Chinese civilians.
